newsitem.title: INDIA: Both "black boxes" found after India mid-air crash.
newsitem.headline: Both "black boxes" found after India mid-air crash.

text.p: Searchers have found the so-called "black boxes" that might explain why two planes collided in mid-air near New Delhi, killing some 350 people, officials said on Wednesday.

"We have recovered both the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder," Indian Director of Air Safety V.K. Chandna told Reuters at the site where a Saudi Arabian Airlines jumbo plummeted to earth in flames.
"They look damaged, but we expect the insides to be safe and secure," he said.
The recorders from the other plane involved in the world's worst mid-air collision, a Kazakh Ilyushin IL-76 freighter, were found earlier in the day, Rajiv Bhaskar of KazAir said.
The two crash sites are some 10 km (six miles) apart on the north Indian plain 80 km (50 miles) from New Delhi. Chandna said the recorders would be taken to the capital for analysis.
He said the authorities had also sealed recordings made in the control tower pending the appointment of a judicial inquiry into one of the world's five-worst air disasters.
"We have sealed the recordings of the control tower. All that will be taken into account when a judge is appointed to begin the investigation," he said.
There were 312 people aboard the Saudi Boeing 747 and 37 on the Ilyushin chartered from Kazakhstan National Airways, known as KazAir. Most bodies have been recovered, many charred or mangled.

Bhaskar, the KazAir airport manager in Delhi, said the passengers on the IL-76 were businessmen who had chartered it for the flight to New Delhi, where they had planned to buy Indian goods and fly them back home.
He said they were carrying $1.5 million in cash and intended to buy wool items, cheap in India, to sell them at home where the weather is getting colder.
India's Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda headed for the sites on Wednesday.
The Saudi jumbo also crashed in a fireball after taking off from Delhi with a full load of fuel. Bodies were strewn throughout the debris over a wide area.
The Press Trust of India said search teams found two intact bodies -- a mother and child clinging to each other.
Experts offered several possible reasons for the mid-air collision, including inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport, language difficulties and pilot error.
Some said many pilots from the former Soviet Union often had difficulty understanding English, the language of international aviation.
Bhaskar said that was an unlikely explanation.
"If that was the case we would have accidents every other day," he said. "I believe the cause of the collision was either pilot error or control tower error."
He did not comment on suggestions that the pilot of the Kazakh freighter might have miscalculated the conversion into metres of control tower instructions given in feet.
The Saudi plane was told to climb to 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) after taking off for Dhahran and Jeddah.
The KazAir plane, which was coming in to land on the same flight corridor, was instructed to maintain a height of 15,000 feet (4,575 metres), Indian aviation officials said.
Experts said altimeters in aircraft in the former Soviet Union were calibrated in metres, unlike most planes elsewhere which were in feet.
Unless the Kazakh aircraft had an altimeter that expressed its height in both measurements, the pilot could have made a mistake in the conversion, they said.
